reply: Based on the aqueous, likely clear cell culture broth, a low‑cost NIR transmission probe is the simplest primary option; Raman could be added later if specificity is insufficient.

risks: Increasing broth turbidity may attenuate the transmission signal, reducing accuracy.
Probe fouling from cells or proteins could require periodic cleaning or replacement.
Chemometric model may drift with changing media composition; regular recalibration needed.

steps: Collect a set of broth samples spanning the expected range of glucose and lactate concentrations.
Measure each sample off‑line (reference assays) and in‑line with the NIR transmission probe.
Develop a multivariate calibration (e.g., PLS) using the paired data.
Validate on independent samples not used in model building.
If transmission signal degrades, repeat steps with a Raman probe for comparison.

Validate the model on samples not used to build it (held-out samples, e.g. from other patients, batches or days) before drawing any conclusion; a model built on few samples can fit them without generalising.
